name: Priya Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do chat and email for FreshCart, the online grocery delivery company, from their contact centre by the ring road. It's missing bananas, squashed eggs, drivers who left the bags at the wrong door, that kind of thing, maybe ninety chats a day. I came from six years of bar work, so I'm only six months in and still slower than the others on the refund rules. I use an AI assistant all day to draft replies and check the policy, and I've built myself a little library of prompts for the weird cases.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The targets wear me out, more than the customers. Ninety chats, a satisfaction score, and a timer in the corner of the screen going red. What I like is the puzzle side, working out what actually happened to somebody's shopping, and the people on my pod, who are funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. Honestly, that would be a bit disappointing. I use these tools every day and they already save me loads of time. If AI only ever saves me time on squashed eggs and missing bananas, that's fine, but I expected more from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's still worth learning the tools, because they make the boring bits faster. Online I'd probably post something like, the hype was overblown but the tools are still good. I'd also say the time saved should go to staff, not more chats per hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good news for my job. I'd keep my place at FreshCart and probably get better faster, because the assistant covers my gaps on the policy stuff. The thing I'd watch is management using it to bump the target from ninety to a hundred and ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, using the assistant for every draft and sharing my prompt library with the pod. I'd put another five hundred a month into the index fund I started last year. And I'd ask my team lead, Rosa, if I could run a short session for new starters on the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. My money's fine, Jonas has a steady job at the hospital, and I'm not worried about this version at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tool covers your gaps. Has anyone at work noticed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa, my team lead, told me last month I'm the only new starter whose scores went up in week three. That's the tool, really, not me, and I'm happy to say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You worry about the target going up. Has that happened before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it already happened once, in summer. They raised it to a hundred chats because the assistant was saving time. I'd push back, but I'd do it with numbers, not just complaining.

say: The tools are still **worth learning**, because they speed up the boring bits.
Any time saved should go to **staff**, not more chats per hour.
think: This is **good news** for my job at FreshCart.
The real risk is managers raising the **chat target** again.
do: Keep using the **assistant** for every draft and share prompts with the pod.
Add **£500 a month** to the index fund started last year.
Offer to run a **tools session** for new starters.
feel: **Calm**, with solid savings and Jonas's steady **hospital job**.
S0.quote: If AI only ever saves me time on squashed eggs and missing bananas, that's fine, but I expected more from it.
fieldNote: Priya is the rare junior who **gains** from AI, using it to cover her inexperience.
She separates the **tool** from how management uses it.
She'd fight targets with **numbers**, a calm, practical style of protest.
Her **strong savings** and partner's job remove money worry here.

steps.text: Run a session on the AI assistant for FreshCart's new starters
Add £500 a month to her index fund
Keep handling ninety grocery chats a day as normal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that's basically my prediction. Customer chats about missing items are perfect for a bot. Half my day would go in the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's be the ones who shape it, not the ones it happens to. I'd say we need a staff forum, or the union, at the table when they decide which chats go to the bot. Online I'd post about fair transitions, and how the gains should be shared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be OK, because I'd move into the team that trains and checks the bot. But I'm a bit uneasy about saying that, because lots of my pod won't get that chance. I'd feel guilty being the one who's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Within a month I'd apply to whatever team runs the bot, testing answers and fixing the bad ones. I'd do an evening course in conversation design, which is writing how bots talk, about six hundred quid online. And I'd help start a staff forum at FreshCart, because there isn't a union at our site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, a bit guilty. It's exciting for me and rubbish for people like Dev on my pod.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your pod do you think about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev's forty-one, he's been there eight years and he hates computers. My pod mate Dev is brilliant on the phone with angry people. I can't see the new grocery delivery firm having a place for Dev, and that's not fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you sure the bot team would want you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not exactly. I think it's more that my job would change and I'd go with it. If I'm wrong and the bot team is tiny, I've got savings and lots of other places nearby to apply.

say: Let's **shape the change** instead of having it happen to us.
A **staff forum** or union should help decide which chats go to the bot.
think: I'd be **OK**, moving into the team that trains and checks the bot.
I'd feel **guilty**, because most of my pod won't get that chance.
do: Apply to the **bot team** within a month to test and fix answers.
Take a **conversation design** course online for about £600.
Help start a **staff forum** at FreshCart's site.
feel: **Hopeful** about her own path, and **guilty** about colleagues left behind.
S1.quote: My pod mate Dev is brilliant on the phone with angry people. I can't see the new grocery delivery firm having a place for Dev, and that's not fair.
fieldNote: Priya expects her **job to change**, not vanish, and she moves toward the change.
Her mood is shaped by **colleagues' risk** more than her own.
She'd build a **staff forum** where no union exists, matching her progressive views.
Her fallback of **savings and nearby jobs** keeps her steady.

steps.text: Apply to FreshCart's bot-training team within a month
Take a £600 online course in conversation design
Help start a staff forum at the FreshCart site

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for everything? That's a different story. The bot team would only last until the bot can check itself, which in that world is quite quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments acting now, not after: a pause on mass layoffs, a basic income, something. I'd post a lot, I know I would. I'd say it's not a tech problem, it's a who-gets-the-money problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared for the first time. My trick has always been, learn the tools before everyone else. If the tools can do all of the thinking, being early doesn't save you. It just means you see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at FreshCart as long as I could and save harder, a thousand a month instead of five hundred. I'd apply for jobs at AI companies doing human review, because those would be the last thinking jobs. And I'd volunteer with a campaign group pushing for a basic income, properly, not just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My savings would carry us for over a year, and Jonas is a nurse, so the hands-on side keeps him going for a while. But my plan for life was built on being quick to learn, and that doesn't work here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Jonas say about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas thinks the hospital will need people to sit with patients for a long time, robots or no robots. I hope he's right. If he is, we'd be a one-salary house for a bit, and we could do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the review jobs go too, what's your next move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. Maybe something with people, face to face, but I'd have to think. Bar work, ha. Honestly, I'd go back to a pub before I'd sit at home.

say: Governments need to act **now**: pause mass layoffs and look at a **basic income**.
It's not a tech problem, it's a **who-gets-the-money** problem.
think: For the first time, being **early** with tools doesn't protect me.
My job at FreshCart would likely **go**, and so would the bot team.
do: Raise savings from £500 to **£1,000 a month** while still employed.
Apply for **human review** roles at AI companies.
feel: **Anxious** and shaken that her usual strategy no longer works.
Some comfort that Jonas's **nursing job** lasts longer.
S2.quote: My trick has always been, learn the tools before everyone else. If the tools can do all of the thinking, being early doesn't save you.
fieldNote: Fast AGI breaks Priya's core belief that **adapting early** keeps her safe.
Jonas's **hands-on job** makes them a one-salary household she can live with.
She'd fall back to **bar work** rather than stay idle, which fits her past.
Her politics turn from posting to **volunteering**.

steps.text: Double savings to £1,000 a month while still at FreshCart
Apply for human review jobs at AI companies
Volunteer with a campaign for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I can work with that. The bot team gives me a few years, and then I'd want to be somewhere else by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to my pod: start now, don't wait for the letter. I'd post about it, and I'd push FreshCart to pay for training for everyone, not just the keen ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine, as long as I move early. But I'd want the next move to be something AI doesn't do well, something with people in a room. I've been thinking about counselling for ages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd join the bot team and start a part-time counselling certificate, two evenings a week. I'd keep using the AI tools every day, because they'd pay my way for the next few years. And I'd lobby FreshCart, with the forum, for a training fund for the whole floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. It's the version where my way of doing things still works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would the counselling course cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two thousand, and it takes two years. I'd pay it from savings without blinking. Jonas would tease me, since I was the one who said I'd never study again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why counselling? Couldn't AI do that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Counselling is people in a room, talking about the worst moments of their lives. I don't think anyone wants a robot for that. And robots for hands-on work come around 2034 anyway, but counselling isn't really hands-on, it's being there.

say: **Start now** and don't wait for the redundancy letter.
FreshCart should pay for **training for everyone**, not just the keen ones.
think: I'll be **fine** if I move early.
My next job should involve **people in a room**, like counselling.
do: Join the **bot team** and use AI daily to earn through the transition.
Start a **counselling certificate**, two evenings a week, for about £2,000.
Lobby FreshCart through the forum for a **training fund**.
feel: **Pretty good**, because her approach of moving early still works.
S3.quote: Counselling is people in a room, talking about the worst moments of their lives. I don't think anyone wants a robot for that.
fieldNote: Five years lets Priya plan a **two-step move**: bot team, then counselling.
She would pay for training **herself** without hesitation.
She stays **uneasy** rather than calm, because the chat job still ends.
She keeps pushing for **training for all**, not just herself.

steps.text: Start a two-year part-time counselling certificate
Join FreshCart's bot team and keep using AI daily
Push the staff forum for a training fund for all

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years? That's loads. I'd be thirty-seven by the time it lands, and probably on a totally different path by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we have no excuse. Governments, firms, unions, everyone should be planning now. I'd post about a shorter working week as the way to share it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's great for me. I'd grow with the tools and then move on to counselling well before 2036. My worry is more the people who'll hear ten years and switch off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the five-year version, just calmer. I'd do the conversation design course this year and counselling in a year or two. I'd keep five hundred a month going into the index fund. I'd still help run the staff forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, even. Ten years is enough to have two careers. I'd grow with the AI tools at work and then move on to counselling well before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the index fund feel odd, given your politics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. Index funds would mostly be big tech in the end, so I'd be partly betting on the thing I'm worried about. I've made peace with that, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this change anything at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Jonas and I want kids in a few years, and ten years of warning makes that easier, not harder. We'd go ahead around thirty, I think.

say: We have **no excuse** with ten years; everyone should be planning now.
A **shorter working week** is the fair way to share out the gains.
think: This is **great for me**: I'll grow with the tools and then move on.
The risk is people hearing **ten years** and switching off.
do: Take the **conversation design** course this year.
Start **counselling training** in a year or two.
Keep adding **£500 a month** to the index fund.
feel: **Calm** and even **excited** at the chance of two careers.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to have two careers. I'd grow with the AI tools at work and then move on to counselling well before 2036.
fieldNote: With a decade, Priya feels **calm and excited**, the brightest of her five answers.
She admits the **index fund** bets on big tech, which sits uneasily with her politics.
She'd keep **family plans** with Jonas on track.
Her concern turns to others who will **switch off**.

steps.text: Take the conversation design course, then counselling training
Keep adding £500 a month to the index fund
Plan to have children with Jonas around age thirty

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's the only one where being quick and curious doesn't help, and that's all I've got. What would help is a basic income, or at least a decent wage while people retrain, and firms being made to share the savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who's actually deciding. On the floor it's managers and spreadsheets, never us. A staff forum at FreshCart helped, but it's still a long way from being in the room. If customer service workers don't get a seat when firms decide what the bots do, the bots will be built to cut us, not help us.

headlineQuote: If customer service workers don't get a seat when firms decide what the bots do, the bots will be built to cut us, not help us.
portrait: Priya, **27**, does chat and email at **FreshCart** after six years of bar work.
She uses an **AI assistant** all day and leans on it to cover her inexperience.
She lives with Jonas, a **nurse**, and has strong savings and an index fund.
She stays **calm or uneasy** in slower pictures, but fast AGI breaks her **move-early** strategy.
Her long plan is **counselling**, and she always pushes for colleagues' training too.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because being **quick** to learn no longer helps.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or paid retraining, with firms made to share the **savings**.
